food.text: The Three Sisters are squash, maize and climbing beans, grown together by many Native American groups. Maize and beans were planted in mounds of hilled soil, with squash between them. The cornstalk acts as a trellis for the beans, the beans fix nitrogen, and squash leaves shade the ground to keep it moist.
Around 600, the Hohokam of the Southwest began cultivating agave on large areas of rocky, dry ground. Agave became a major food source that supplemented the food grown in irrigated areas.

Maize is thought to have been introduced to the Cahokia region around AD 900, and it is often credited with driving the city's early growth. Yet more recent research suggests that diets at Cahokia were quite varied, especially in its early period.

Before Mississippian culture took hold, Woodland peoples mainly used crops of the Eastern Agricultural Complex. Mississippians emphasized maize, but they kept using the older crops too. The period between 900 and 1000 also saw an uptick in maize consumption.

From 800 AD, Three Sisters crop organization was used at Cahokia. Squash, gourds and maize were first grown alongside wild beans, and domesticated beans did not appear there until 1250. The resulting food surplus supported Cahokia's expanded population. But the surrounding woodlands were cleared through overuse, runoff repeatedly flooded the crop fields during the growing season, and by c. 1350 the site had been mostly abandoned and its large population dispersed.

At Cahokia, goosefoot and sumpweed from the Eastern Agricultural Complex were grown and eaten. Thomas Emerson and Kristin Hedman explain individuals with low-maize diets as members of hunter-gatherer immigrant communities that had not yet adopted maize as a staple.

Hohokam seeds and grains were prepared on stone manos and metates. Their pots of unembellished brown, which appeared shortly before 300 CE, were used for storage and cooking, and also as containers for cremated human remains.

art.text: Effigy mounds are raised piles of earth built in the shape of stylized animals, symbols, or human and religious figures. The Effigy Moundbuilder culture is primarily associated with the years 550 to 1200 CE. The Wisconsin Historical Society has identified over 3200 animal-shaped effigy mounds in the upper midwest.

Around 800 CE, Basketmakers in Chaco Canyon were building crescent-shaped stone complexes. Each had four to five residential suites next to subterranean kivas, large enclosed areas reserved for rites. Such structures characterize the Early Pueblo People.

Monks Mound is the largest Pre-Columbian earthwork in the Americas and the largest pyramid north of Mesoamerica. Its construction began between 900 and 955 CE. Its base is roughly the same size as that of the Great Pyramid of Giza.

In Chaco Canyon, Chacoan builders quarried sandstone blocks and hauled timber from great distances. They assembled 15 major complexes that remained the largest buildings in North America until the 19th century. Chaco was a major cultural center between 900 and 1150.

Unlike Egyptian pyramids built of stone, Monks Mound was constructed almost entirely of layers of basket-transported soil and clay. Because of its flattened top it retains rainwater, which has caused slumping. Recent excavations show slumping was a problem even while the mound was being made.

Pueblo Bonito is the largest and best-known great house in Chaco Culture National Historical Park. Ancestral Puebloans occupied it between AD 828 and 1126. It was planned and built in stages and was the center of the Chacoan world.

The Alligator Effigy Mound in Granville, Ohio, was likely built around AD 950, based on radiometric dating of charcoal from its base. Brad Lepper suggests it depicts an underwater panther, a powerful figure in Native American myth. He thinks early European settlers misinterpreted what Native Americans told them: they were told it was a fierce creature that lived in the water and ate people, which the settlers assumed to be an alligator.

The Caddoan Mississippians built earthwork platform mounds, often used for temples, arranged around large, level plazas. The plazas were usually kept swept clean and used for ceremonies involving large groups. By 800 CE some villages were becoming prominent ritual centers.

Pueblo Bonito's Room 33 held the richest burial ever excavated in the Southwest. A man who died violently was buried with thousands of turquoise and shell beads and pendants, which originally formed necklaces, anklets and bracelets. Archaeologists believe the room was built as a crypt for him and his descendants.

Strong evidence shows a canyon-wide turquoise processing and trading industry in Chaco Canyon from the tenth century. Around then, the first section of Pueblo Bonito was built: a curved row of 50 rooms near its present north wall.

Nelson Reed, a local businessman and historian of native cultures, began excavating Monks Mound in the 1960s, hoping to find the high-status building presumed to have stood at its peak. His drilled cores revealed the mound's construction stages from the 10th to 12th centuries CE. No temple was found.

In 2009, traces of Mexican cacao from at least 1,200 miles away were detected in pottery sherds at Pueblo Bonito. The substance was important in rituals. It shows the far-reaching connections of the Chacoan world.

science.text: The Hohokam of what is now Arizona built the most complex canal network in the pre-contact Western Hemisphere, around modern Phoenix. Engineering improved their access to river water, and they excavated canals to irrigate crops in the Sonoran Desert.

The Ancestral Puebloans held a distinct knowledge of celestial sciences that found form in their architecture. They lived across the Four Corners region, where their communities were linked in a complex network of hundreds of settlements.

By about 1000 CE, the Hohokam were the first to master acid etching. They daubed shells with pitch and bathed them in acid, most likely made from fermented cactus juice. Artisans also produced jewelry from shell, stone, and bone.

From 800 AD, Three Sisters crop organization was used at Cahokia, the largest Native American city north of the Rio Grande. The Three Sisters are squash, maize and climbing beans, and their cultivation produced a food surplus large enough to support Cahokia's expanded population. Overuse of the surrounding land later degraded it: woodlands were cleared, runoff flooded the fields during the growing season, and by c. 1350 Cahokia was mostly abandoned.

The Post-Hopewell Late Woodland period was characterized by new bow and arrow technology and an uptick in maize consumption. Between 900 AD and 1000 AD, the Emergent Mississippian period began shell-tempered pottery production and platform mounds topped with summit structures.

In Three Sisters companion planting, the cornstalk serves as a trellis for climbing beans. The beans fix nitrogen in their root nodules, and the wide leaves of the squash plant shade the ground, keeping the soil moist and helping prevent weeds.
The Caddoan Mississippians acquired the bow and arrow from peoples of the Southwest by 500 CE. Pottery making had been introduced to them earlier by peoples to their East.

Mound building at Cahokia began with the emergent Mississippian cultural period, around the 9th century CE. Its inhabitants left no written records beyond symbols on pottery, marine shell, copper, wood and stone, but the evidence of an elaborately planned community, woodhenge, mounds and burials reveals a complex and sophisticated society. In Mound 72, archaeologists found the remains of about 270 individuals, and scholars believe almost 62% of the other skeletons there were sacrificial victims, judging by signs of ritual execution and method of burial.
Hohokam evidence of trade networks includes turquoise, shells from the Gulf of California, and parrot bones from central Mexico. Seeds and grains were prepared on stone manos and metates.

politics.text: By 800 CE, early Caddoan society began to coalesce into one of the earlier Mississippian cultures. Some villages became ritual centers, where workers were organized to build earthwork platform mounds, often used for temples, along with elite residences.

The Mississippian period began at the end of the 10th century in the Southern United States and the Eastern Woodlands. Its peoples were characterized by theocratic governance, population centers and maize agriculture. Their Woodland predecessors had mostly limited mound building to burial mounds.

At Pueblo Bonito in Chaco Canyon, analysis of nine skeletons from high-status graves showed that members of an elite matriline were interred for approximately 330 years, between 800 and 1130. This suggests continuity with the matrilineal succession practices of many Pueblo nations today.

The Post-Hopewell Late Woodland period saw new forms of political organization. Between 900 AD and 1000 AD, the Emergent Mississippian period began building summit structures on platform mounds, and Cahokia began to grow.
Between 900 and 1000 CE, the Emergent Mississippian period began building summit structures on platform mounds. It also began producing shell-tempered pottery and saw the growth of Cahokia.

By 1000 CE the Caddoan society had a more stratified hierarchy, with some lineage and kin groups exerting more control over the community. Leaders were buried in tombs with elaborate grave goods. When such a leader died, there were sacrificial "retainer" deaths, and both family members and followers were killed and buried with them.

In the centuries before 1000 CE, populations in the American Bottom lived in small settlements of 50 to 100 people, used for only 5 to 10 years. By the end of the 10th century, many of these settlements had aggregated into larger groups.
Room 33 in Pueblo Bonito is the richest burial ever excavated in the Southwest. It served as a crypt for one powerful lineage, traced through the female line, for approximately 330 years.

The Miller culture of the upper Tombigbee River area built large platform mounds at sites such as Pinson Mounds, which archaeologists speculate were for feasting rituals. By the end of the Late Woodland period, about 1000 CE, the Miller culture area was absorbed into the succeeding Mississippian culture.

philosophy.text: By 800 CE, early Caddoan society was coalescing into one of the earlier Mississippian cultures, and some villages began to gain prominence as ritual centers. Workers built earthwork platform mounds, often used for temples, arranged around large plazas.

In the centuries before 1000 CE, settlements in the American Bottom began to be built along cosmologically organizing principles. Their layouts emphasized the cardinal directions and distinct sectors of society, showing how ideas about the cosmos shaped everyday space.
The Mississippian peoples grew out of Woodland groups and inherited the Hopewell clan system. In it, each clan functioned like a ritual society rather than solely a kin group.
The larger villages that formed around Cahokia by the end of the 10th century included earlier cosmogram layouts. These layouts came complete with large central posts, pits, and structures.

During the Pueblo I period (750 to 900 CE), Ancestral Puebloan buildings stood closer together and reflected deepening religious celebration. Towers were built near kivas and were likely used as look-outs.

As complex religious and social ideas developed among the early Caddoans, some people and family lineages gained prominence over others. The archaeological record marks this with large tombs holding exotic grave offerings that were obvious symbols of authority and prestige.

culture.text: L'Anse aux Meadows in Newfoundland is a Norse settlement with carbon dating estimates between 990 and 1050 CE. Its eight buildings were built of sod over a wood frame. The largest dwelling measured 28.8 m by 15.6 m and had several rooms.

Around 800, Basketmakers in the Chaco Canyon area were building crescent-shaped stone complexes. Each had four to five residential suites abutting subterranean kivas, which were large enclosed areas reserved for rites.

By 800 CE, early Caddoan society began to coalesce, and some villages became ritual centers. Workers built platform mounds, often used for temples, arranged around large plazas. The plazas were usually kept swept clean and used for ceremonies involving large groups of people.

Cahokia, as it is now defined, was settled around 600 CE during the Late Woodland period, and mound building there began around the 9th century CE. Its inhabitants left no written records beyond symbols on pottery, marine shell, copper, wood and stone.

At the Grewe-Casa Grande site, groups of pithouses were arranged around small circular plazas along the Coolidge Canal system in the sixth century CE. By the eighth century it had become a summer home for the priests and chieftain. A medium-sized ballcourt adjoined its large central plaza.

Workshops at L'Anse aux Meadows included an iron smithy with a forge and iron slag, and a carpentry workshop that generated wood debris. A specialized boat repair area contained worn rivets. Three small buildings may have housed lower-status crew or slaves.

The sagas describe Vinland as having a river and a lake with abundant fish. They specifically mention salmon larger than any the Norse had seen before. The grapes and wheat mentioned are thought to be native grapes and sandwort.

By 1000 CE, tomb burials of people thought to be Caddoan leaders were accompanied by elaborate grave goods. At the death of such leaders there were sacrificial "retainer" deaths and burials of both family members and followers.
